title: SRE Documentation Standards: SLOs, Capacity, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Reviews, Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary:

This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for:
- Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budget management
- Capacity planning and forecasting
- Reliability initiatives and prioritization
- Incident review (postmortem) standards
- Operational tooling and observability expectations
- Runbook templates and ownership

Purpose and audience:
This guidance is intended for SREs, service owners, and on-call engineers responsible for production reliability. It standardizes how we define SLOs, track error budgets, plan capacity for model-serving workloads, run reliability initiatives, and conduct incident reviews.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Goals and scope:
- All externally visible customer-facing services (hosted API, Dedicated control plane, data-plane gateways) must define at least two SLOs: availability and end-to-end latency for a representative request class.
- Internal infra services (e.g., build systems, CI) should define appropriate SLOs aligned with consumers.

SLO format (required fields):
1. Service name (e.g., inference-api-v2)
2. Owner (team and on-call alias)
3. SLI definition (measurement method, query, aggregation)
4. SLO target (percentage over a rolling period) and measurement window
5. Measurement backend (Prometheus/Thanos, Datadog metric id, PerfEdge)
6. Error budget policy and mitigation actions

Recommended SLO targets (examples):
- Availability (region-level): 99.95% over 30 days for hosted API production traffic.
- P99 latency (generate-streaming): 250ms for control-plane RPCs, 500ms for tail end-to-end token latency for short requests (<=128 tokens).
- Embeddings batch latency (95th): 300ms for typical batch sizes under Dedicated capacity commitments.

Error budget policy (standardized):
- Green (>=90% remaining): normal deploys and experiments allowed.
- Yellow (50-90% remaining): require SRE review for risky deploys; limit batch/large model experiments.
- Orange (10-50% remaining): freeze non-critical deploys; prioritize reliability work; increase alerting cadence.
- Red (<10% remaining): immediate mitigation; rollback recent changes that consumed budget; schedule reliability-focused maintenance and communicate to stakeholders.

Operationalizing SLIs and SLOs:
- SLIs must be implemented as executable queries with documented thresholds and a link to the dashboard panel. Include the exact query used (PromQL/Datadog).
- All SLOs must be registered in the SRE SLO registry (internal dashboard) with links to alerts, runbooks, and owner contact.
- Configure continuous alerting for SLO burn rate (1h/6h/24h windows) and error-budget thresholds.

2) Capacity Planning and Forecasting

Principles:
- Capacity planning prioritizes predictable latency and throughput for model inference workloads while optimizing cost.
- Use traffic-based forecasting (ingestion from API gateway), model characteristic baselines (seq length, kv-cache usage), and scheduled/seasonal growth assumptions.

Required artifacts for each service:
- Capacity roadmap (12 month) with expected growth scenarios (baseline, +30%, +100%).
- Runway calculation: current capacity, committed Dedicated contracts, and expected deprecation of legacy hardware.
- Emergency scale playbooks: steps to provision temporary burst nodes, re-route traffic to compatible cheaper model variants, and use fallback regions.

Capacity planning cadence and owner responsibilities:
- Monthly capacity review: SRE + infra + product review forecasts and incidents that indicate mis-provisioning.
- Quarterly forecast refresh: update 12-month plan with recent telemetry and sales/usage commitments.
- Owners: service owner prepares forecasts; infra capacity lead validates hardware availability and procurement timelines.

Key thresholds to track:
- GPU utilization percentiles (p50/p95 on batching nodes) - alert when sustained p95 > 75% for 6 hours.
- Queue length and prefetch hit ratios - alert when queue length grows beyond expected SLAs.
- Cold-start rate for auto-scaled pods - alert when cold-starts exceed 5% of requests over 1 hour.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

Initiative process:
1. Identification: from incidents, SLO misses, or architectural risk scans.
2. Triage: SREs perform RCA and estimate cost of delay and impact to SLOs.
3. Prioritization: triage in Reliability Council (monthly) - rank by expected SLO improvement and engineering effort.
4. Execution: assign owner, set milestones, measure pre/post metrics.

Examples of typical initiatives:
- KV cache hotkey mitigation to reduce tail latency for chat workloads.
- Better prefix-caching for repeated prompt patterns to reduce token compute.
- Automated canary routing and rollback for model weight updates.

Success criteria and measurement:
- Each initiative must include one or more measurable success criteria (e.g., reduce P99 by X ms, increase availability by Y%, reduce GPU token cost by Z%).
- Post-implementation monitoring window of 30 days to validate impact.

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems)

Scope and timeline:
- A postmortem is required for any incident that meets one of: customer-visible outage, SLO breach, Severity >= Sev2, or significant cost event.
- Postmortem template due within 72 hours; final review and RCA published within 14 days.

Postmortem structure (required fields):
- Title and incident summary (short, one paragraph)
- Timeline of events (UTC timestamps)
- Impact (users affected, services impacted, error budget consumption)
- Root cause analysis (contributing factors, primary cause)
- Actions and owners (short-term mitigation, medium-term fixes, long-term prevention)
- Follow-up verification plan (how we'll confirm remediation)
- Blameless summary and lessons learned

Action tracking and verification:
- Actions must be tracked in the Reliability Initiatives board with owners and due dates.
- Verification tasks tagged "verification" and closed only after the 30-day monitoring window confirms the fix.

5) Operational Tooling and Observability

Minimum tooling expectations for services:
- Metrics: request rate, error rate, latency (p50/p95/p99), capacity (GPU utilization, queue length), and request-level cost estimate.
- Traces: distributed tracing with sample rate sufficient to investigate 95% of incidents; include model name, model-version, shard-id, and request-id in spans.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with severity, request_id, trace_id, and user_tenant_id where applicable.
- Dashboards: owner-maintained dashboard with SLO panels, burn-rate alerts, and capacity health.

Recommended integrations and workflows:
- Automated SLO burn notifications into on-call Slack channel when burn crosses yellow threshold.
- Runbook jump links from alerts to the primary runbook and the incident playbook.
- Nightly health checks and weekly SLO digest emails to service owners.

Operational access and data retention:
- Logs and traces retention: default 30 days for high-cardinality logs, 90 days for aggregated metrics.
- Sensitive payloads: must be redacted at ingestion for hosted API (see security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention for policy).

6) Runbooks: Template and Best Practices

Runbook purpose:
- Provide a concise actionable playbook for on-call responders to safely triage and mitigate common issues without requiring deep exploratory work.

Required runbook sections (flat list for easy parsing):
- Title and service: one-line description
- Pager severity definition and typical symptoms
- Quick checks (1-min): health-check URLs, leader status, queue length, GPU utilization, recent deploys
- Short-term mitigations (safe actions): restart flaky pods, enable fallback model routing, scale up worker pool (CLI commands provided)
- Long-term fixes / RCA pointer: link to associated initiative or ticket
- Owner and escalation path: primary on-call, secondary, engineering manager, product owner
- Postmortem link (if incident triggered the runbook)

Runbook example (abridged):
- Service: inference-api-v2
- Symptom: Increased 95th/99th latency for generate requests
- Quick checks:
  1. Verify SLO dashboard panel and burn rate
  2. Check GPU node p95 util: prometheus query: avg_over_time(gpu_utilization[5m]) by (instance)
  3. Check request queue length (metric: inference_queue_length)
- Safe mitigations:
  - Route 10% traffic to model-variant-fallback using /admin/route-toggle CLI (example provided)
  - Scale horizontal workers: k8s scale deployment inference-worker --replicas=$(($(kubectl get deploy inference-worker -o=jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}')+5))
  - Temporarily reduce tokenizer batch sizes via feature-flag toggle

Ownership, review cadence, and lifecycle
- Runbooks must be reviewed quarterly by the service owner and the on-call rotation owner.
- Each runbook must include the last-reviewed date and reviewer name.

Appendix: Example SLO table (text table)
| Service | SLI | Window | Target | Measurement backend | Owner |
| inference-api-v2 | availability (5xx) | 30d | 99.95% | prometheus:service:availability | inference-team-oncall |
| inference-api-v2 | p99 latency (generate <=128 tokens) | 30d | 500ms | datadog:metric:p99_generate | inference-team-oncall |

Checklist for new services (onboarding):
- [ ] Register SLIs in SLO registry with executable queries and dashboards
- [ ] Create capacity forecast and runway doc (12 months)
- [ ] Provide runbook and link to alerting rules
- [ ] Verify logs/traces/metrics instrumentation and retention policy
- [ ] Add to monthly capacity review agenda

Governance and exceptions:
- Exceptions to these standards must be approved by the SRE Director and documented with an expiration.
- Services with restricted data or compliance constraints may have modified observability/retention; coordinate with security-and-compliance.
